title: Elliptical Galaxy NGC 5363 and Spiral Galaxy NGC 5364
caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 5363 and spiral galaxy NGC 5364, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Two very different galaxies occupy opposite corners of this image in the constellation Virgo. In the upper left is NGC 5363, an elliptical galaxy, and in the lower right is NGC 5364, a spiral.

An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of mostly older stars with little of the gas and dust needed to make new ones. A spiral galaxy, by contrast, is a flattened disc with arms that wind out from the center, where much of its star formation takes place.

These two are likely in the early stages of a gravitational interaction. As galaxies draw closer, their mutual pull can distort their shapes and stir up gas. Pairs like this one give astronomers a chance to see how interactions begin, long before any merger.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used three filters. B is shown in blue, V in green and I in red.
